questions.stem: Which is an assumption of a perfectly competitive market?
options: A few large firms supply most of the output sold in the market
Each firm sells a product that is slightly different from its rivals'
New firms face very high start-up costs to enter the market
Buyers and sellers have perfect knowledge of prices and products
questions.explanation: Perfect competition assumes many buyers and sellers, identical products, perfect knowledge and free entry and exit. Differentiated products are a feature of monopolistic competition, and a few dominant firms describe an oligopoly.

questions.stem: In a perfectly competitive market, each firm is a 'price taker'. This means that:
options: it charges whatever price the government regulator sets for the market
it can raise its price without losing any of its existing customers
it must accept the market price, as it is too small to influence it
it sets its price by adding a profit margin to its costs of production
questions.explanation: With many sellers of an identical product, a single firm that charges above the market price loses its customers to rivals, so it has to take the price the market sets. Adding a margin to costs is price setting, which requires some market power.

questions.stem: A market has many sellers of an identical product, but a licence system limits the number of new sellers. Which assumption of perfect competition does it fail?
options: freedom of entry and exit
a large number of buyers and sellers
homogeneous (identical) products
perfect knowledge of the market
questions.explanation: A licence that caps the number of sellers is a barrier to entry, so the market fails the assumption of free entry and exit. It still has many sellers and identical products, so those assumptions are met.

questions.stem: The law of demand states that, other things being equal:
options: as the price of a good rises, the quantity supplied falls
as the price of a good rises, the quantity demanded falls
as the price of a good rises, the quantity demanded rises
as the demand for a good rises, its price falls
questions.explanation: The law of demand describes an inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded, giving a downward-sloping demand curve. A rise in demand raises price rather than lowering it, and quantity supplied is described by the law of supply.

questions.stem: Which best explains why the demand curve slopes downwards?
options: at lower prices, sellers are willing to supply a larger quantity of the good
at lower prices, buyers assume the quality of the good has also fallen
at lower prices, firms advertise more heavily and attract new buyers
at lower prices, buyers can afford more and switch from dearer substitutes
questions.explanation: A lower price lets buyers' incomes stretch further and makes the good cheaper relative to substitutes, so quantity demanded rises. Sellers supplying more at higher prices, not lower ones, is the law of supply.

questions.stem: With all else unchanged, a fall in the price of petrol causes:
options: a movement up along the demand curve for petrol
a movement down along the demand curve for petrol
a shift of the demand curve for petrol to the right
a shift of the demand curve for petrol to the left
questions.explanation: A change in the good's own price moves buyers along the existing demand curve; a lower price means a movement down it to a larger quantity demanded. Only a change in a non-price factor shifts the curve.

questions.stem: The price of butter rises sharply. What happens in the market for margarine, a substitute?
options: demand for margarine decreases, shifting its demand curve left
the quantity of margarine demanded rises along its demand curve
the supply of margarine decreases, shifting its supply curve left
demand for margarine increases, shifting its demand curve right
questions.explanation: When a substitute becomes dearer, some buyers switch to margarine at every price, so its demand curve shifts right. The price of margarine itself has not changed, so this is a shift, not a movement along the curve.

questions.stem: The price of gaming consoles falls substantially. What is the most likely effect in the market for console games?
options: demand for games falls, so their price and quantity both fall
the supply of games rises, so their price falls and quantity rises
the quantity of games demanded rises along an unchanged demand curve
demand for games rises, so their price and quantity both rise
questions.explanation: Consoles and games are complements, so cheaper consoles bring more console owners, which raises demand for games at every price. The demand curve shifts right, raising equilibrium price and quantity; the price of games did not change first, so it is not a movement along the curve.

questions.stem: Interest rates on home loans rise. In the market for newly built houses, the most likely effect is that:
options: demand falls, as borrowing to buy a house becomes more expensive
demand rises, as savers earn more interest on their bank deposits
supply rises, as builders earn higher returns on their own loans
quantity demanded falls along an unchanged demand curve for houses
questions.explanation: Most buyers borrow to purchase a house, so higher interest rates raise the cost of buying and reduce demand at every price. Interest rates are a non-price factor, so the effect is a shift of the demand curve, not a movement along it.

questions.stem: Income tax cuts raise households' disposable income. For a normal good such as restaurant meals, this will:
options: cause a movement along the demand curve
shift the demand curve to the left
shift the demand curve to the right
shift the supply curve to the right
questions.explanation: Higher disposable income means households will buy more of a normal good at every price, so demand shifts right. Tax cuts for households do not change restaurants' costs, so supply is unaffected.

questions.stem: Consumer confidence falls sharply after reports of rising job losses. Demand for new cars is most likely to:
options: decrease, as households delay large purchases they can put off
increase, as households buy before car prices rise any further
increase, as lower confidence pushes down the price of cars
decrease, as car makers respond by cutting their output of cars
questions.explanation: When households fear for their jobs, they postpone big, deferrable purchases such as cars, so demand shifts left. Car makers cutting output is a change in supply, which does not explain a fall in demand.

questions.stem: Australia's population is ageing. Which market is most likely to see its demand curve shift right as a result?
options: first-home loans
aged care services
childcare places
school uniforms
questions.explanation: An ageing population means a larger share of older people, which raises demand for aged care at every price. Childcare and school uniforms are bought mainly for young children, whose share of the population is shrinking.

questions.stem: A widely reported study links a popular breakfast cereal to health problems. In the market for that cereal:
options: demand falls, lowering the equilibrium price and quantity
supply falls, raising the equilibrium price and lowering quantity
demand falls, lowering the price but raising the quantity sold
quantity demanded falls, but the equilibrium price is unchanged
questions.explanation: The study changes tastes and preferences, shifting demand left, so both equilibrium price and quantity fall. Nothing has changed producers' costs or technology, so supply does not shift.

questions.stem: Which change would cause a movement along the demand curve for beef, rather than a shift of it?
options: a rise in the price of lamb, which is a substitute for beef
a rise in the disposable incomes of Australian households
a health campaign encouraging people to eat less red meat
a fall in the price of beef after a large rise in cattle supply
questions.explanation: When supply rises, the price of beef falls and buyers move down the existing demand curve. The price of a substitute, incomes and tastes are non-price factors, so each would shift the demand curve itself.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly uses the terms 'demand' and 'quantity demanded'?
options: A rise in the price of a good reduces the demand for it.
A rise in incomes raises the quantity demanded of a normal good.
A fall in the price of a good increases the demand for it.
A rise in the price of a good reduces its quantity demanded.
questions.explanation: A change in a good's own price changes the quantity demanded, a movement along the curve. 'Demand' refers to the whole curve, which shifts only when a non-price factor such as income changes, so higher incomes raise demand, not quantity demanded.

questions.stem: The law of supply states that, other things being equal:
options: as the supply of a good rises, its market price rises
as the price of a good rises, the quantity demanded rises
as the price of a good rises, the quantity supplied rises
as the price of a good rises, the quantity supplied falls
questions.explanation: The law of supply describes a direct relationship between price and quantity supplied, giving an upward-sloping supply curve. An increase in supply lowers the equilibrium price rather than raising it.

questions.stem: Why does the supply curve usually slope upwards?
options: higher prices lower the cost to firms of producing each extra unit
higher prices attract more consumers into the market for the good
higher prices make production more profitable, so firms offer more
higher prices reduce demand, so firms must offer more to make sales
questions.explanation: At a higher price, producing extra units becomes profitable even where their costs are higher, so firms supply more. Higher prices do not lower costs, and attracting consumers concerns demand, not supply.

questions.stem: Wages in the clothing manufacturing industry rise. In the market for locally made clothing, this will:
options: cause a movement along the supply curve
shift the supply curve to the right
shift the supply curve to the left
shift the demand curve to the left
questions.explanation: Wages are a cost of production, so higher wages make each unit dearer to produce and supply shifts left. Price has not changed first, so this is a shift rather than a movement along the curve.

questions.stem: Wheat farmers adopt a new seed variety that raises yields per hectare. The most likely effect in the wheat market is that:
options: demand increases, raising both the price and the quantity sold
supply decreases, raising the price and lowering the quantity
supply increases, lowering the price and raising the quantity
supply increases, raising both the price and the quantity sold
questions.explanation: Better technology raises output from the same resources, so supply shifts right, the equilibrium price falls and quantity rises. A rightward supply shift cannot raise the price, because it creates a surplus at the old price.

questions.stem: A severe drought in New South Wales and Queensland reduces the cotton harvest. In the cotton market:
options: supply shifts left, so price rises and quantity falls
demand shifts left, so price and quantity both fall
supply shifts right, so price falls and quantity rises
quantity supplied falls along the existing supply curve
questions.explanation: Climatic conditions are a non-price factor, so drought shifts the supply curve left, raising the equilibrium price and lowering quantity. The price did not change first, so the effect is a shift of supply, not a movement along it.

questions.stem: Productivity in a car parts factory rises. This means that:
options: workers are paid more for each hour, shifting the supply curve left
more output is produced per unit of input, shifting supply right
more inputs are needed for each unit of output, shifting supply left
the price of car parts rises, shifting the demand curve to the right
questions.explanation: Productivity is output per unit of input; when it rises, the cost of each unit falls and supply shifts right. Higher productivity can support higher wages, but productivity itself measures output per input, not pay.

questions.stem: Which change causes a movement along the supply curve of lamb, rather than a shift of it?
options: a fall in the cost of the feed used to raise lambs for meat
a flood that drowns large numbers of sheep in rural Victoria
a new processing technology that cuts the cost of producing lamb
a rise in the price of lamb after demand for lamb increases
questions.explanation: When demand increases, the price of lamb rises and farmers move up their existing supply curve. Feed costs, floods and processing technology are non-price factors, so each shifts the whole supply curve.

questions.stem: At a price above equilibrium, the market will have:
options: a surplus, which puts downward pressure on price
a shortage, which puts upward pressure on price
a surplus, which puts upward pressure on price
a shortage, which puts downward pressure on price
questions.explanation: Above equilibrium, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded, so unsold stock builds up and sellers cut prices. A shortage occurs below equilibrium, where buyers compete for too few goods and bid the price up.

questions.stem: In a market for festival tickets, at $20, 100 are demanded and 40 supplied; at $30, 80 and 60; at $40, 70 and 70; at $50, 60 and 85. At a price of $30, the market has:
options: a surplus of 20 tickets, so the price will tend to fall
a shortage of 60 tickets, so the price will tend to rise
a shortage of 20 tickets, so the price will tend to fall
a shortage of 20 tickets, so the price will tend to rise
questions.explanation: At $30, 80 tickets are demanded but only 60 supplied, a shortage of 20, so buyers bid the price up towards the $40 equilibrium. Sixty is the quantity supplied, not the size of the shortage.

questions.stem: In the market for electric cars, consumer preferences shift towards them while battery costs fall. The equilibrium quantity will:
options: rise, and the equilibrium price will definitely fall as well
fall, but the change in price cannot be known without more information
rise, but the change in price cannot be known without more information
rise, and the equilibrium price will definitely rise as well
questions.explanation: Demand and supply both shift right, so quantity rises for certain. Demand pushes the price up and supply pushes it down, so the change in price depends on which shift is larger.

questions.stem: A frost cuts the world coffee crop at the same time as a fashion for coffee raises demand. In the coffee market:
options: price will fall, but the change in quantity is uncertain
quantity will rise, but the change in price is uncertain
both the equilibrium price and quantity will fall
price will rise, but the change in quantity is uncertain
questions.explanation: Supply shifts left and demand shifts right, and both push the price up, so price rises for certain. Supply's shift lowers quantity while demand's raises it, so the change in quantity depends on the sizes of the shifts.

questions.stem: In a market, demand increases slightly while supply increases by a much larger amount. Compared with the original equilibrium:
options: quantity rises and price rises
quantity falls and price falls
quantity falls and price rises
quantity rises and price falls
questions.explanation: Both shifts raise quantity, so quantity rises. The large rise in supply pushes the price down by more than the small rise in demand pushes it up, so the price falls overall.

questions.stem: After demand for a good rises, the market is in shortage at the old price. The market returns to equilibrium as:
options: price rises, shifting the supply curve to the right until it clears
price rises, shifting the demand curve back to the left until it clears
price rises, lowering quantity demanded and raising quantity supplied
price falls, raising quantity demanded and lowering quantity supplied
questions.explanation: A shortage leads buyers to bid the price up, which moves buyers up along the demand curve and sellers up along the supply curve until the quantities are equal. A change in the good's own price causes movements along the curves, not shifts.

questions.stem: In a market economy, a rise in the relative price of a good signals to producers that:
options: the good is less highly valued, so resources should move out of producing it
the government wants the good to be produced in smaller quantities from now on
the costs of producing the good have fallen, so the profit from making it is lower
the good is more highly valued, so resources should move into producing it
questions.explanation: A higher relative price means producing the good is more profitable, which draws land, labour and capital into producing it. This signalling role of prices is how the market mechanism allocates resources without central direction.

questions.stem: The price of lithium rises sharply relative to the prices of other minerals. In a market economy, the most likely response is that:
options: the government directs mining firms to produce more lithium
consumers buy more lithium because it is now more valuable
mining firms move land, labour and capital into lithium production
mining firms reduce lithium output so that its price stays high
questions.explanation: The higher relative price raises the profit from lithium, so firms shift resources into producing it. In a market economy, the price signal does this without government direction; a higher price lowers the quantity buyers demand rather than raising it.

questions.stem: Over a year, the price of strawberries rises by 5% while the general price level rises by 8%. The relative price of strawberries has:
options: stayed the same, because strawberry prices and other prices both rose
fallen, because strawberry prices rose more slowly than prices overall
risen, because the price of strawberries increased by 5% over the year
risen, because prices overall increased by 8% over the same year
questions.explanation: A relative price compares one good's price with others. Strawberries became dearer in dollars, but cheaper compared with other goods, so their relative price fell, and the market signals that less of society's resources should go to them.

questions.stem: Demand for plant-based milk rises strongly. Which sequence best describes how the market mechanism reallocates resources?
options: price falls, more consumers buy it, and firms choose to produce less
price rises, profits rise, existing firms expand and new firms enter
price rises, profits fall, existing firms leave the market for good
government sets a higher price, and firms expand on its instruction
questions.explanation: Higher demand raises the price, which lifts profits and signals firms to expand and new firms to enter, moving resources into the product. A rise in demand raises the price rather than lowering it, and the market mechanism works without government direction.

questions.stem: A market with a single seller of a product that has no close substitutes, protected by high barriers to entry, is:
options: monopolistic competition
perfect competition
a monopoly
an oligopoly
questions.explanation: A monopoly has one seller, no close substitutes and high barriers that keep rivals out. An oligopoly has a few large sellers rather than one.

questions.stem: Which feature is characteristic of an oligopoly?
options: Many small firms sell identical products at the market price
Many firms sell slightly different products, with easy entry
One firm supplies the whole market, with no close substitutes
A few large firms dominate, and each reacts to the others' decisions
questions.explanation: In an oligopoly a few large firms dominate, so each must consider how rivals will respond, which is called interdependence. Many firms selling differentiated products with easy entry is monopolistic competition.

questions.stem: A suburb has dozens of cafés, each offering a slightly different style of coffee and atmosphere, and new cafés open easily. This market is best described as:
options: monopoly
monopolistic competition
perfect competition
oligopoly
questions.explanation: Many sellers, differentiated products and low barriers to entry describe monopolistic competition. It is not perfect competition, because the cafés' products differ, which gives each a little control over its price.

questions.stem: Compared with a perfectly competitive market, a monopoly is most likely to:
options: charge a lower price and produce a larger quantity
charge a higher price and produce a larger quantity
charge the same price but offer consumers less choice
charge a higher price and produce a smaller quantity
questions.explanation: A monopoly can restrict output to raise its price above what competition would allow, earning higher profits. Charging more and selling more at once is impossible along a downward-sloping demand curve.

questions.stem: Why might a high degree of market power lower living standards?
options: firms can restrict output and raise prices, so fewer resources go to goods consumers value
firms must accept the market price, so they cannot afford to invest in new products
competition among many firms forces prices below the costs of producing the goods
consumers are given too much choice, so they end up buying goods they do not need
questions.explanation: Firms with market power can charge more and produce less than competitive firms, so resources are not allocated to where consumers value them most, and consumers pay more. Accepting the market price describes price takers in perfect competition, who have no market power at all.

questions.stem: In an oligopoly, firms often avoid price wars and compete through advertising and loyalty schemes instead. The main reason is that:
options: the government prevents firms in an oligopoly from changing their prices
each firm in an oligopoly is a price taker and cannot set its own price
products in an oligopoly are identical, so firms cannot use price to compete
a price cut by one firm is likely to be matched by rivals, cutting everyone's profits
questions.explanation: Oligopolists are interdependent: if one cuts its price, rivals usually match it, so no firm gains customers and all earn less. Non-price competition lets a firm win customers without triggering that response. Oligopolists are price setters, not price takers.

questions.stem: Which is the best example of a barrier to entry?
options: consumers having full information about the prices of every seller
a fall in the cost of renting shop space in a shopping centre
the very high cost of building a national mobile phone network
a large number of small firms already selling the same product
questions.explanation: A huge set-up cost deters new firms, so the few existing firms keep their market power. Many small existing sellers, full information and cheaper shop rents all make entry easier, not harder.

questions.stem: An airline charges travellers who book a day before departure far more than those who book months ahead, for the same economy seat. This strategy is:
options: multiple branding
price fixing
resale price maintenance
price discrimination
questions.explanation: Charging different groups of customers different prices for the same product, where the difference is not due to cost, is price discrimination. Price fixing needs an agreement between competitors, which a single airline setting its own fares is not.

questions.stem: A large company sells several brands of laundry detergent that compete on supermarket shelves, each aimed at a different group of buyers. This strategy is called:
options: exclusive dealing
market sharing
multiple branding
price discrimination
questions.explanation: Multiple branding is one firm selling several brands of a similar product, capturing different segments and creating the appearance of more competition than exists. Price discrimination involves different prices for the same product, not different brands.

questions.stem: Three building firms secretly agree on which of them will submit the lowest bid for each government contract. Under the Competition and Consumer Act 2010, this is:
options: price discrimination, which is generally legal
multiple branding, a type of product strategy
misuse of market power by a single large firm
bid rigging, a form of cartel conduct
questions.explanation: Competitors agreeing in advance who will win a tender is bid rigging, one of the forms of cartel conduct the Act prohibits, alongside price fixing, market sharing and restricting output. Misuse of market power involves one firm acting alone, not an agreement between rivals.

questions.stem: Under the Competition and Consumer Act 2010, which conduct is prohibited?
options: a company selling two competing brands of the same product
a newly opened café cutting prices to win customers from rivals
competing firms agreeing to divide up customers by region
a cinema charging lower prices to students and pensioners
questions.explanation: An agreement between competitors to share markets is cartel conduct, which the Act prohibits. Concession pricing, multiple branding and ordinary price competition by a small new entrant are lawful strategies.

questions.stem: The main purpose of the Competition and Consumer Act 2010 is to:
options: set the minimum wages paid to workers in each industry
set the prices of all goods and services sold in Australia
regulate the interest rates that banks charge borrowers
promote competition and fair trading and protect consumers
questions.explanation: The Act aims to improve the welfare of Australians by promoting competition and fair trading and protecting consumers, and the ACCC enforces it. Minimum wages are set by the Fair Work Commission, and the Act does not set the prices of goods.

questions.stem: In a regional town, one of three petrol stations closes. The remaining two soon charge similar prices and rarely change them independently. This market is best described as:
options: monopolistic competition, because the two stations are differentiated
an oligopoly, where interdependent firms may avoid price competition
a monopoly, because there is no longer any competition in the town
perfect competition, because both stations charge the same price
questions.explanation: With only two sellers who watch and match each other's prices, the market is an oligopoly with strong interdependence. Charging the same price does not make a market perfectly competitive; that needs many sellers who are price takers.
